raw_text:
{"builder": {"source": "x", "name": "Dan Shipper", "handle": "danshipper", "bio": "ceo @every | the only subscription you need to stay at the edge of AI", "tweets": [{"id": "2120539547620790424", "text": "I look at what I do with Fable 5.2 in the cracks of my week and think: this would've taken five people and $200,000.

Then I look at what my team does with the same AI.

Last week, between meetings, I analyzed our customer survey, made a game for our team, spotted an opportunity to sell @Every to teams, built a CRM, and started reaching out.

Look at that and you might ask: Why would I need a team at all?

The chart seems to agree. On OpenAI's GDPval benchmark, AI went from beating human experts 12.4% of the time in 2024 to around 83% in 2026. That's the aggregate view of the future of work: gather a lot of data and extrapolate a trend line.

But the aggregate misses something. To see it, you have to get intimate: zoom in on one real situation, with all its messiness, and extrapolate from there.

We gave everyone at Every access to the same customer survey and the same AI models.

• I found an opportunity to sell to teams.
• @poojary_yash saw that first-time subscribers were churning because we send too much email.
• @dabrundage noticed that many of our readers feel lonely: they're excited about AI, but people around them think they're crazy.
• @jackcheng turned the results into a Claymation game show.

Could you ask Claude to produce what each of them found? Maybe. But generating possibilities is cheap. Knowing which ones matter is hard.

@hammer_mt ran an experiment to predict what I'd say in Slack. When Claude got 400 attempts, it produced an answer like mine 93% of the time. But when it had to rank its own answers, mine landed in its top 10% only around 60% of the time.

Each person on a team is responsible for a different part of the world. That responsibility narrows where they look, and their perspective helps them decide what matters enough to act on. A team explores more possibilities than a single default prompt, and it can take responsibility for what it finds.

The obvious objection: models will get better at ranking. I think they will. But people aren't frozen while that happens. Comparing 2026 Yash with 2027 Claude misses that there will also be a 2027 Yash, with another year of experience, using 2027 Claude.

As models improve and spread, they raise the floor for everyone. The default answer becomes the baseline. The value is in using your perspective and responsibility to push past it.

That's why I think we need to change how we measure AI. Instead of only asking how well a model performs on problems everyone agrees are worth solving, ask: How good is it at doing my work, from my perspective?

The aggregate can show us the capability curve. The intimate helps us see what we might build, and who we might become, as we ride it.

raw_text: Hey, welcome back to the Every Podcast, where we talk about the future of work. I'm Natalia Quintero, and at Every, our team of writers and builders use AI every day, so we can tell you how the frontier is shifting, what actually works, and what you need to know. So last week at Every, we hosted our first ever conference, V.C.S.S., It was a full day of talks in Brooklyn featuring speakers from Anthropic, OpenAI, Notion, Lovable, Ode, and many more. If you missed it, we'll have all of the talks available at every.to forward slash TV. We built the whole day around one question. What does great human work look like after automation? Dan Shipper, Every's co-founder and CEO, closed the conference with his answer, which you'll hear later in this episode. He took our quarterly customer survey results and built a custom CRM, then a video game, and then personally reached out to a pretty vast number of our customers. In pre-AI terms, he did the work of about five people, a data scientist, a game developer, a marketer, an engineer, and a salesperson. But instead, he did all of that work with a single clot subscription over the course of a single week. And if you ask Claude what it sees in the same survey, you'll probably get a generic answer that anyone could get. And that's actually Dan's point. Great work is the perspective you bring to the model. So for the podcast this week, Dan's closing talk from our conference thesis. Enjoy. Thesis, did everyone have a good time? Woo! Well, we gathered here to answer one question, which is what is the future of great human work after automation? I hope you got some good answers today. Did you get some good answers? Yes? Yes? All right. I wanna add my take. Hopefully I can help bring it together a little bit. So I really, I love this question. And obviously, because we built the conference around it, it's really the question that we try to answer every day at every, And what's really interesting about this question is you're really trying to predict the future. And there's two, I think, real methods for predicting the future. One is what I'll call the aggregate, where you gather lots and lots of data, and then you extrapolate a trend line. And the other is called the intimate, where you zoom in on one real case or real situation, and then you extrapolate from there. And in our culture, we tend to emphasize the aggregate. The aggregate is objective, it's quantitative, and the intimate kind of feels a little bit anecdotal. And the aggregate's also extremely powerful. The reason we have AI is the aggregate, is for example, scaling loss. We found that if you put more data and compute on one end of the system, you get more capability out.
